questions.question: Name the four economic sectors and place each stage of the wool chain — shearing, weaving, retailing and fibre research — into its correct sector.
questions.expected_answer: Primary extracts raw materials from nature; secondary transforms raw materials into products; tertiary provides services; quaternary works with knowledge and information. Shearing wool on the Karoo farm is primary, weaving it into cloth at the mill is secondary, selling the coat and couriering it is tertiary, and breeding finer-woolled sheep at a research station is quaternary.

questions.question: Distinguish GDP from GNP using an example, and state the approximate share each sector contributes to South Africa's GDP.
questions.expected_answer: GDP totals everything produced inside a country's borders regardless of ownership; GNP follows ownership — production by a country's citizens and companies anywhere in the world. A British-owned bank in Sandton counts in South Africa's GDP but Britain's GNP: the ground versus the passport. Shares: agriculture about 2,5–3 per cent, mining under 10 per cent, the secondary sector roughly a fifth, and the tertiary sector close to two thirds — a services-dominant structure.

questions.question: Explain why agriculture's share of employment is nearly double its share of GDP, and state the general rule this gap illustrates.
questions.expected_answer: Raw farm produce sells cheaply, keeping agriculture's money share small, but farming is still labour-intensive — harvesting and packing need many hands at modest wages — so its employment share is far larger. General rule: labour-intensive sectors hold a bigger share of employment than of GDP, while capital-intensive, high-value-per-worker sectors such as finance hold a bigger share of GDP than of employment.
